To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the use of a visual journey through a hospital system, as experienced by people with dementia and their family carers, is an effective tool to identify the barriers to optimal care and to develop strategies to overcome them.
“People living with dementia and family carers are able to describe the elements of an ideal journey through the health-care system and identify areas for improvement in the current system.”.

(1) people living with dementia are often excluded from the health‐care decision‐making process; (2) people living with cognitive impairment are not always provided with adequate support to participate in health‐care decisions; and (3) people living with a dementia diagnosis may experience significant barriers in their ability to make informed decisions about their health care.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the everyday practices of care and support for people with dementia and their families.
the organisation of care and the practices of care, and the ways in which these practices can be improved.
the everyday lives of people living with cognitive impairment and dementia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

this special issue provides a rich resource for understanding the complex issues that are involved in the organisation of care and practice for people living with dementia in Australia, and the role that research can play in improving the quality of that care.
this is a collection of papers that are all worth reading and that together they provide a rich source of insights into dementia care.
this is a well‐written, well‐researched, and well‐argued piece of work.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have been able to develop a model of partnership research that has generated new knowledge about dementia, and that has been able to be translated into practice and policy.
the partnership approach to research, care and support for people living with dementia has been a success.

the CDPC has provided a platform for a range of projects that have generated new knowledge and evidence to support the implementation of evidence‐based practice and the translation of research into practice.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the CDPC has demonstrated that it is possible to develop a research program that is responsive to the needs of the community, and to the concerns of those who live with, and provide care for people living with dementia in the context of everyday life.
we must continue to work together to improve dementia care, to improve quality of life, and to improve the lives of people living with and affected by dementia.
the CDPC has shown how a research‐ practice‐ consumer partnership can be established and maintained over an extended period.
